newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Foreigners flee Sierra Leone after coup.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners flee Sierra Leone after coup.

text.p: Evacuation of foreigners from Sierra Leone gathered pace on Thursday while the new military authorities struggled to consolidate their control.

British and other European nationals gathered at a beachside hotel to take helicopters across the wide river estuary to Lungi airport, from where a chartered Boeing 747 was due to leave for Paris and London in the afternoon.
U.S. Marines and helicopters from the U.S. Navy ship Kearsarge landed to evacuate Americans.

The evacuation of foreigners staying in a few overcrowded hotels in the steamy, seaside capital has taken on added urgency because of moves by Nigeria to reverse Sunday's military coup, which has been condemned internationally.

On Wednesday, a helicopter chartered by Belgian carrier Sabena flew 130 people to Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea. A Boeing 707 plane sent by Lebanon evacuated 178 Lebanese, most of them women and children. It also carried the bodies of two Lebanese men killed in the coup.
A U.N.-chartered boat carried 97 people to Conakry and was expected to make a second trip on Thursday.

The new military authorities who seized power on Sunday blamed harassment of civilians on former servicemen and escaped prisoners in army uniform and warned they would be arrested, apparently oblivious to the fact that the most prominent escaped prisoner was new head of state, Major Johnny Paul Koromah.

Koromah, 33, was among those freed from Freetown's Pademba Road prison early on Sunday at the start of the coup. He was detained on treason charges over an earlier alleged coup attempt against civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who flew to Guinea on Sunday.

Koromah's Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) set up hotlines for the public to complain about harassment and looting, though it was unlikely many people would risk reporting looting which witnesses say is carried out mainly by soldiers.
"The AFRC is appealing to all Sierra Leoneans to cooperate with the Army to restore peace, law, and order in our beloved country," a statement said. "Your complaints will be thoroughly investigated."

West African military sources acknowledged that a steady buildup of Nigerian troops was part of a regional plan to reinstate Kabbah. No military move was expected until the evacuations were completed, the sources said.
"I think that is one of the things holding up a quick strike against the coup leaders," said one source.
A Nigerian Air Force Hercules C-130 plane flew two missions from neighbouring Liberia on Wednesday to land combat troops and supplies at Lungi.

Three Nigerian frigates docked in Freetown with troops on Tuesday to bolster the West African ECOMOG peacekeeping contingent that was based in Sierra Leone when low-ranking soldiers seized power on Sunday.
Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha has been denounced in the West for his faltering plan to end army rule in his own country and his government's human rights record.

But he has won reluctant credit for pressing on with a costly regional peacekeeping mission in Liberia which has a mandate that extends to helping the Sierra Leone government in a fight against rebels.

Despite Washington's strong disapproval of Abacha's government, U.S. State Department spokesman John Dinger said the Nigerians had been playing a "useful role" in Sierra Leone as leader of the ECOMOG force.
Nigeria is the backbone of the Economic Community of West Africa Monitoring Group (ECOMOG) which was first sent to Liberia in 1990.
